And yet, yet, the entire earthly figure he produces is a new creation by virtue of the absurd. He resigned everything infinitely, and then he grasped everything again by virtue of the absurd. He continually makes the movement of infinity, but he does it with such correctness and certainty that he constantly comes out of it with finitude, and there is not a second when one suspects anything else. The most difficult task for a dancer is supposed to be to leap into a definite posture in such a way that there is not a second when he is grasping for the posture, but in the leap itself he stands in the posture. Perhaps no dancer can do it — but this knight does. The mass of people live lost in worldly sorrow and joy; these are the wallflowers, who do not come into the dance. The knights of infinity are dancers and have elevation. They make the movement upward and fall down again, and this too is no unblessed pastime, and not unlovely to look upon. But every time they come down again, they cannot at once assume the pose; they waver a moment, and this wavering shows that, for all that, they are strangers in the world. The wavering is more or less striking, depending on their skill; but even the most skillful of these knights cannot conceal that wavering. One does not need to see them in the air; one need only see them at the moment they touch and have touched the earth — and one knows them. But to be able to come down in such a way that the very second one looks as though one were standing and walking, to transform the leap of life into a walk, to absolutely express the sublime in the pedestrian — that only this knight can do — and this is the only wonder.

modern_text: The historical catastrophe was, according to Aristotle, the following: in order to revenge themselves, the family slip a temple-vessel in among his household goods, and he is condemned as a temple-robber. Event scarce went off without tears; were a poet to adopt it, he might surely count upon sympathy. Is it not dreadful that love, which often enough hath been an exile in life, is now also robbed of heaven's assistance? Is not the old saying that marriage is established in heaven here put to shame? Otherwise it is all the troubles and difficulties of finitude that, like evil spirits, would sunder the lovers, while love hath heaven on its side, and therefore this holy alliance vanquisheth all foes. Here it is heaven itself which sundereth what heaven itself hath, after all, joined together. Who would also have suspected this? least of all, surely, the young bride. Only a moment ago she sat in her chamber in all her beauty, and the lovely girls had conscientiously decked her out, so that they could answer for it before all the world, so that they had not only joy thereof but envy — yea, joy that it was impossible for them to be more envious, because it was impossible for her to be more beautiful. She sat alone in her chamber, and was transformed from beauty to beauty; for all that womanly art could achieve was used worthily to deck the worthy; but there was still wanting somewhat which the young girls had not dreamed of: a veil, finer, lighter, and yet more concealing than that in which the young girls had wrapped her — a bridal robe of which no young girl knew, or could be of help to her in. This, however, is a matter of indifference; for the question is not whether the family is shrewd or stupid in taking revenge — the family acquireth only ideal significance insofar as it is drawn into the hero's dialectic. It is, moreover, fateful enough that he, in seeking to flee the danger by not marrying, plungeth into it, and that his life in a twofold manner cometh into contact with the divine, first by the augur's saying, next by being condemned as a temple-robber.

source_text: For faith is precisely this paradox: that the single individual is higher than the universal, yet, mark well, in such a way that the movement repeats itself — that is, that having been in the universal, he now, as the single individual, isolates himself as higher than the universal. If this is not faith, then Abraham is lost; then faith has never existed in the world, precisely because it has always existed. For if the ethical, i.e., the moral, is the highest, and there is nothing incommensurable left in a person except in such a way that this incommensurable is evil, i.e., the singular which is to be expressed in the universal, then one needs no other categories than those Greek philosophy possessed, or those that can be drawn out of these by consistent thinking. This Hegel ought not to have concealed; for he had, after all, Greek studies behind him.
modern_text: For faith is precisely this paradox, that the single individual is higher than the universal — yet, mark well, in such a way that the movement repeats itself, that, having been in the universal, he then, as the single individual, isolates himself as higher than the universal. If this be not faith, then is Abraham lost; then hath faith never been in the world, precisely because it hath always been. For if the ethical, that is, the moral, be the highest, and there remain in man nothing incommensurable in any other way than that this incommensurable is evil, that is, the single, which is to be expressed in the universal, then one needeth no other categories than those which Greek philosophy possessed, or those which by consistent thinking may be drawn out of these. This Hegel ought not to have concealed; for he hath, after all, had Greek studies.

source_text: There was once a man who, as a child, had heard that beautiful tale of how God tested Abraham, and how Abraham endured the temptation, kept the faith, and a second time received a son against all expectation. When he grew older, he read the same story with even greater admiration; for life had separated what had been united in the pious simplicity of the child. The older he grew, the more often his thoughts turned to that tale; his enthusiasm became stronger and stronger, and yet less and less could he understand the story. At last he forgot everything else over it. His soul had only one wish: to see Abraham. One longing: to have been a witness to that event. His desire was not to see the beautiful regions of the East, not the earthly glory of the promised land, not that god-fearing couple whose old age God blessed, not the venerable figure of the aged patriarch, not the vigorous youth of the Isaac whom God had granted — he had no objection to the same thing taking place on a barren heath. His craving was to ride along on those three days when Abraham rode with sorrow before him and Isaac at his side. His wish was to be present in that moment when Abraham lifted his eyes and saw Mount Moriah in the distance, the moment when he left the asses behind and went up the mountain alone with Isaac. For what occupied him was not the artful weaving of the imagination, but the shudder of thought.
modern_text: Once upon a time there was a man who, as a child, had heard that beautiful tale of how God tempted Abraham, and how Abraham stood firm in the temptation, kept the faith, and a second time received a son against expectation. When he grew older, he read the same tale with still greater wonder; for life had divided what had been united in the child's pious simplicity. The older he grew, the more often his thought turned to that tale; his enthusiasm waxed stronger and stronger, and yet less and less could he understand the tale. At last he forgot all else for its sake; his soul had but one wish — to see Abraham — and one longing, to have been a witness of that event. His desire was not to behold the beautiful regions of the Orient, not the earthly glory of the promised land, not that god-fearing married couple whose old age God blessed, not the venerable figure of the aged patriarch, not the vigorous youth of Isaac whom God bestowed — he had nothing against its all taking place upon a barren heath. His craving was to accompany them on the three days' journey, when Abraham rode with sorrow before him and Isaac at his side. His wish was to be present in the hour when Abraham lifted up his eye and saw the mountain of Moriah in the distance, the hour when he left the asses behind and went on alone with Isaac up to the mountain; for what occupied him was not the artistic weaving of the imagination, but the shudder of thought.
